items.title: Jean Bach interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: Well Chubby Jackson has a rule about the basses.

ctx.x: We had a similar story from, I forget who told it now, about Illinois Jacquet doing the same thing in Europe. The sound man went through the whole thing, set the levels, and then Illinois said, “now take all your faders and turn them down 50 percent, and don’t touch them again.”

Yes. Well Chubby Jackson has a rule about the basses. Because they’ve suddenly, it’s the democratization in action, you know, democracy in action. They all, everybody wants to be heard, and so they turn that thing up very high. And Chubby said, “when it goes past this direction, it’s too loud.” And yeah, I hate amplification. It’s not what we were used to. It’s not the natural sound, it’s something else.
Right. I guess if you’re playing big stadiums or auditoriums, there’s a certain level.

items.title: Chubby Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: And a lady by the name of Jean Bach put this whole thing together, a lovely lady, too

ctx.x: Yeah. Because all these guys were in that photo. And that wasn’t called “Great Day in Harlem.” And a lady by the name of Jean Bach put this whole thing together, a lovely lady, too, and whoever was available — I mean Woody was not there because he was out of town, Lionel wasn’t there, Duke wasn’t there. But if you see that picture, I have a little picture of that with me—
